analysis.one_liner: Exempts non-invasive diagnostic devices from Food and Drug Administration regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal law so that diagnostic devices that do not pierce or enter the body, such as wearable monitors and some at-home testing devices, would no longer be regulated by the FDA. Makers could sell those devices without proving they work or are safe. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of non-invasive diagnostic devices gain the most: they could sell products without FDA review, without proving accuracy, and without the cost and delay of the approval process. Consumers could buy such devices, but with no federal check on whether the results are reliable.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the definition of a medical device in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to carve out any 'non-invasive diagnostic device,' removing it from FDA's regulatory authority. [S3]

A device qualifies as non-invasive if it does not penetrate the skin or any body membrane, is not inserted or implanted, causes only brief compression or temperature changes to tissue, and exposes tissue to no ionizing radiation. [S2]
Device makers would avoid the cost, time, and evidentiary requirements of FDA device review for this whole category of products. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who use these devices bear the risk: a diagnostic device could give wrong results, and neither the company nor the FDA would be required to catch it before sale. Doctors and health systems that rely on patient-reported test results also inherit the uncertainty.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers relying on unregulated test results

drawbacks.text: FDA review is the main public check that diagnostic devices actually measure what they claim; exempting an entire category removes that check even though diagnostic errors can lead to missed or wrong treatment. [S2]
The definition is drawn broadly enough to cover a wide range of wearables and at-home testing devices, so the exemption would not be limited to genuinely trivial products. [S2]
The bill offers no replacement oversight, such as truth-in-labeling or post-market tracking, for the devices it removes from regulation. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster, cheaper market entry for device makers; the cost is that consumers get no independent assurance that a diagnostic device works. A diagnostic device that quietly gives wrong answers can cause real harm, so the trade as written favors industry over the people using the products. The bill also drew no support from either party, suggesting the design did not persuade even sympathetic lawmakers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, got zero cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on May 19, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day. [S5]
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee and received no hearing, markup, or floor vote. [S5]
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people are no worse off, because the FDA kept the authority it would have lost to oversee diagnostic devices. The bill's sponsor and the industry it would have benefited gained nothing from its failure.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan pattern: Biggs was its only sponsor and not one member of either party cosponsored it. [S4]

industries.industry: Makers of non-invasive diagnostic devices (wearable monitors, at-home tests)
industries.note: The bill would have freed this industry from FDA review entirely, letting it sell diagnostic products without proving they work. It failed, so the industry keeps operating under existing device rules. Its interest in the bill ran against the public's interest in reliable test results.

Companies in the broader device industry were unaffected; only the non-invasive diagnostic category was targeted for exemption. Devices that pierce the body or use radiation would have stayed regulated.
